paras: The reported lynching of Bald Knobber witnesses was a November 1888 telegraph story that five men who had testified against the Bald Knobber leader Dave Walker had been hanged by former members of the band on Bull Creek in Christian County, Missouri. A detailed special from Ozark named the dead and described about 200 disguised riders, but on the same day a messenger from Bull Creek said no one had been lynched. No confirmation followed, and a Springfield resident later called the story "an unmitigated hoax."

Walker, called the Bald Knobber "king" or chief, had been convicted of murder, and the Missouri Supreme Court had just ruled that he must hang; the Sun gave the date as Dec. 28. According to the Sun, the crime was the August 1887 killing of Charles Edens and William Green at the Edens homestead, and four or five of the prisoners had turned State's evidence.

On the morning of Nov. 15 a rumor reached Springfield that five of the witnesses against Walker had been lynched by "ex-Bald Knobbers" on Tuesday night on the banks of Bull Creek. The dispatch added that nothing authentic had been learned, since the place was forty miles from a telegraph station. Its only named source was a man called Grant, who had come from Taney City to warn Joe Inman and Charles Graves, two State's witnesses, not to return home; he knew of the lynching only from a fleeing relative of Inman.

A separate special from Ozark, sent through Kansas City, gave a fuller version. It said a farmer named James Wilson had come to Ozark for five coffins, and that the bodies of Charles Green, James Eden, William Enders, Jonathan Wiley and Emmett Anderson had been found hanging from an oak near the scene of the 1887 killings, each with a knife-cut across the brow. In this account Green and Eden were lured out at midnight and surrounded by about 200 disguised riders, Wiley's door was broken down while his family fired on the raiders, and Anderson was seized on the road from Chadwick. Sheriff Williams was said to have gone to the scene with a large posse.

Denials came the same day. A Kansas City Times special reported that a man just arrived from the Bull Creek neighborhood found everything quiet and believed the rumor arose from the warning given to Inman. A messenger who reached Ozark from Bull Creek said the men had not been lynched and that nothing exciting had happened there for weeks. No report of bodies identified, an inquest, burials or arrests appears in the coverage.
On Nov. 23 A. M. Haswell of Springfield wrote to the New-York Tribune that the story was a hoax and that the court's ruling had been welcomed in the county as "just and wise."

Coverage was confined to the white press and ran in two strands. The Springfield rumor appeared as "Reported Lynching" in the Alexandria Gazette and as "Lynched by Bald-Knobbers" in the Indianapolis Journal and Memphis Appeal, the Appeal adding "Lack of Particulars." The Sun called it "a thrilling piece of news that is yet to be confirmed," and the Seattle Post-Intelligencer and Salt Lake Herald printed the denial alongside it.

The Ozark special drew the most dramatic treatment. The St. Paul Globe wrote of "five corpses" swinging in the breeze and a country "again under a reign of terror," while the Beatrice Daily Express headed it "Terribly Avenged" and the Press and Daily Dakotaian "Missouri Bald Knobbers Again at Their Murderous Work." Weeklies kept printing the lynching as fact well after the denial: the Emporia Weekly News and Independent Statesman ran the rumor on Nov. 22, the Willimantic Journal and Springfield Weekly Republican on Nov. 23, and the Wahpeton Times the full Ozark account on Nov. 29.

Whether anyone was killed is disputed: only the Ozark special reported bodies, while the Springfield dispatch admitted it had nothing authentic and the Bull Creek messenger and Haswell said nothing happened. The denials came from the reported neighborhood and from a later local letter, while the Ozark version named victims sharing the surnames of the 1887 dead, calling Green and Eden "brothers of the first named."

reader.title: Reported lynching of Bald Knobber witnesses (1888)
bases: Wire reports described five witnesses against Bald Knobber leader Dave Walker as hanged by ex-Bald Knobbers in revenge (A2, A9), though the story was denied the same day (A5, A8) and later called a hoax (A26).

The Ozark special said five men were hanged by about 200 Bald Knobbers (A9), but no confirming report appeared, a Bull Creek messenger and a Springfield resident said no killing took place (A5, A8, A26), and the reported motive was revenge on witnesses rather than a claim of justice (A4).
The rumor and the detailed Ozark special (A2, A9) were contradicted by same-day denials from Bull Creek (A4, A5, A8, A15) and by a Springfield letter calling the story a hoax (A26).
